name: Tin of Sparklers
desc: A biscuit tin of sparklers from York's Bonfire Night. You can write your name in the air with one. Keep well away from the Fieldbook.

name: Turnip Lantern
desc: A hollowed turnip with a face carved in it, lit from inside. This is how it was done before pumpkins came along, and it takes three times as long.

name: Burns Supper Ribbon
desc: A bit of tartan ribbon from a Glasgow Burns Supper, with the haggis course carefully annotated in someone's best handwriting.

name: Daffodil Brooch
desc: A paper daffodil on a safety pin, worn on the first of March. Yellow, optimistic and slightly crushed by a hug.

name: Parade Shamrock
desc: A sprig of shamrock tied with green ribbon, pinned on by a stranger in a very tall hat on St Patrick's Day.

name: Lump of Lucky Coal
desc: A small, clean lump of coal. In Scotland you carry it over the threshold at New Year for luck, which is the one time a lump of coal is a present.

name: May Garland
desc: A ring of fresh leaves and wild flowers, tied with red thread. It smells of spring and slightly of woodsmoke.

name: Wad of Fringe Flyers
desc: A thick wad of flyers for shows you will now feel guilty about not seeing. Among them: a one-woman Hamlet with puppets, and a one-man Hamlet without.

name: Double Gloucester Round
desc: A wheel of Double Gloucester, the cheese they roll down Cooper's Hill. It is mostly very good cheese and slightly dented.

name: Carnival Feather
desc: A long, bright feather from a carnival costume. It is surprisingly heavy when worn for ten hours in the sun, and the dancer insists it was worth it.

name: Pressed-Petal Panel
desc: A small board of wet clay with a picture made entirely of petals, seeds and moss. It took the village four days and it will not survive the bus home.

name: Mari Lwyd Ribbon
desc: A coloured ribbon off a Mari Lwyd's bridle. She is a horse's skull on a pole under a white sheet, and she knocks on doors at midwinter.

name: Guizer's Torch
desc: A burnt-out torch from Up Helly Aa in Lerwick, still smelling of paraffin and triumph. A thousand of them go into the galley in a few minutes, and this one came back.

name: Black Paper Rose
desc: A paper rose, painted black, from Whitby Goth Weekend. It has been worn to the abbey in a gale and looks all the better for it.

name: Eisteddfod Ribbon
desc: A ribbon from the Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod, for a choir that sang bravely and went home with no trophy at all.

name: Tynwald Rushes
desc: A bundle of rushes, strewn on the path to the Tynwald Hill by tradition, tied with a ribbon in the Manx colours.

name: Liberation Flag
desc: A little Jersey flag waved on the ninth of May, the day the German occupation of the Island ended in 1945.

name: Liberation Bunting
desc: A strip of bunting from St Peter Port on Liberation Day, the ninth of May. The Guernsey cross is on every other triangle.

name: Liberation Poppy
desc: A little paper poppy worn in Stanley on the fourteenth of June. Islanders will tell you it is not a day for jokes.

name: Cup Match Pennant
desc: A little pennant for one of the two Cup Match teams. Wear it carefully in the wrong parish, and be prepared to explain.

name: Wee Caber
desc: A caber the length of your forearm, signed by a man built like a wardrobe. It is a very good paperweight.

name: Festival Oyster Shell
desc: A big, clean oyster shell with the year painted on it in white. The champion shuckers keep theirs on the mantelpiece.
